title: Nakamura Leads After Wins Vs. Caruana & Praggnanandhaa
summary: GM Hikaru Nakamura leads by half a point after day one of Clutch Chess: Champions Showdown 2026. He scored two wins in six games with no losses to reach 4/6. GM Javokhir Sindarov, who scored one win and no losses on 3.5 points, is in sole second, followed by GM Fabiano Caruana on 2.5 and GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu on 2. Day two, featuring rounds four-six, is on Wednesday, October 28, starting at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST. Standings Clutch Chess: Champions Showdown returns to the Saint Louis Chess Club for its second edition. Last year, GM Magnus Carlsen won the inaugural tournament, while Caruana came in second. And though Carlsen and World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju have been replaced with Praggnanandhaa and Sindarov this year, the tournament of course remains top-tier. The tournament is a series of three double round-robins; that is, everybody faces everybody with both colors each and every day. The speedy time control of 10+5 allows for a total of 12 games per day. The stakes increase as we approach the end of the event. On the first day, a win is worth $1,000, but on day two it already rises to $2,000—as well as being worth two points rather than one. On day three—you guessed it—it's $3,000 per win and three points. On top of that, the money from all drawn games accumulates each day into a pool (Champion's Jackpot), which is later added to the winner's pot. With seven draws on day one, $7,000 has been added to the winner's prize. Nakamura's lead came as a surprise even to himself, he said on broadcast. "It's a good result, I would say, overall," but he went on: The thing that surprises me is I figured it would be the other way: I feel like everyone else has been super active and they should come out with guns blazing, and it actually seemed the other way around, considering that I haven't played over-the-board in I don't know how long. I feel like everyone else has been super active and they should come out with guns blazing. —Hikaru Nakamura Commentator GM Yasser Seirawan echoed that expectation: "I did not expect Hikaru, who skipped the Grand Chess Tour, to come out and look so good. But he's got to do it all again tomorrow." With a win worth two points on day two, his half-point lead is admittedly a small advantage in the overall race. Even last-place Praggnanandhaa is, after all, two points behind. You can keep reading for our analysis of the games, but you can also check the recap video from the man himself, Nakamura, below. Nakamura's initial win came in the first mini-match, against Caruana. The first game ended in a draw, though Nakamura was briefly winning in the rook endgame, but he then made up for the miss by winning game two. There, the players followed GM Wesley So's playoff game against Caruana from the U.S. Chess Championship—the game that won So the match—but Caruana played the sounder 5...Qe7 this time (instead of the dubious 5...0-0). The queens got traded and the players reached a rather dry endgame, but Nakamura outplayed his opponent with the bishop against a knight (and rooks on the board). 44...Nc4 was the only move; but in the game, 44...Nf7 left the knight on an undefended square, and tactically this made all the difference.

title: 'W' Is For Woodward Wins Titled Tuesday
summary: GM Andy Woodward added his name to the list of Titled Tuesday winners on October 27, scraping by on tiebreaks ahead of GM Arjun Erigaisi despite losing in the first round. GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave came back from a second-round loss to finish third. In case you missed it, here's this week's broadcast with GM Robert Hess: Woodward blundered a checkmate in one move in his very first game, while already ahead by two pawns, but was nearly perfect afterward. And while an unusually high number of 19 players made it to 4/4, the perfect score bounty was gone by the end of round seven. GM Denis Lazavik (who is also playing an over-the-board event in Kazakhstan this week), GM Sergei Zhigalko, and IM Renato Terry all reached 6/6, but all made draws their next game. As a result, they were joined by GM Ian Nepomniachtchi, GM Matthias Bluebaum, and FM Hamidreza Tahmasebi in a six-way tie for first place. That resolved into two spots one round later, with Lazavik and Nepomniachtchi winning their games to set up a clash coming out of the ensuing break. Their game in the ninth round, a rather short draw, was overshadowed by Woodward's shocking rook sacrifices in his contest against GM Dmitry Andreikin. Hess on the commentary was thoroughly impressed.

title: Chess.com Crazyhouse Championship 2026 Starts November 5
summary: Get ready to go wild with your attacks. The Chess.com Crazyhouse Championship is the next event of the Chess.com Community Championships. The event starts on November 5 and features a $2,500 prize fund. Crazyhouse is a chess variant in which players can use their opponent's forces against them. When you capture a piece, it goes into your "bank," and on any turn you can "drop" it back on the board as part of your own army. Because of this, taking the initiative is crucial, and games get extremely sharp from the start. You can get a taste of this variant by watching GM Hikaru Nakamura play Crazyhouse in the video below: The event starts with qualifiers on November 5. Each qualifier is a 75-minute arena with a 3+0 time control. Check the qualifier schedule below to join any arena and participate. Qualifiers Schedule While dirty tactics are encouraged, we expect everyone to play clean. As always, we may ask players to join a fair play call during the qualifiers to ensure a safe playing environment. Players who join the call must set up two cameras from different angles in the room. Refusing to comply will result in the player's removal from the event. The winner of each arena qualifies for the Final on November 6 at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 11:30 p.m. IST. Players will compete in an eight-player double-elimination knockout. Matches are best-of-four with a 3+0 time control. Last year, NM Isaac Chiu won his second Chess.com Community Championship title after defeating IM Mark Plotkin in the Crazyhouse final. Earlier in 2025, the national master had already claimed the crown of the similar Bughouse variant with NM Janak Awatramani, another variant in which captured pieces return to the board. The title also ended IM Nhat Minh To's run of two straight variant championships, Duck Chess and Seirawan Chess. Are you ready to chase your opponent's king in the Chess.com Crazyhouse Championship? Then join the qualifiers on November 5!

title: International conference “Chess in Education” to b­­e held in Almaty
summary: On November 12–13, Almaty will host the 4th International Scientific and Practical Conference “Chess in Education” at Narxoz University. The event is a part of the Comprehensive Plan for the Development of Chess in the Republic of Kazakhstan for 2023–2027, approved by the Government on the instructions of the President of Kazakhstan. The main goal of the conference is to expand the school chess movement, improve teacher training in chess education methodology, and systematically integrate chess into the country’s education system. The conference will be attended by Timur Turlov, President of the International Chess Federation (FIDE) and the Kazakhstan Chess Federation, as well as leading international experts. Speakers include Anzel Laubscher, a member of the FIDE Chess in Education Commission and a senior chess-in-education instructor in South Africa; Dr. Jonathon Quest, visiting associate professor at Webster University; Ali Abbas, President of the Syrian Chess Federation and a FIDE lecturer in chess education; and Ramon Chalmeta Ugas, President of the Catalan Chess Federation and an expert in chess education. The participants will focus on examining the role of chess as an effective tool for developing students’ cognitive skills, critical thinking, and mathematical abilities, as well as practical issues regarding the training of thousands of educators and the integration of chess programs into school curricula. Special emphasis will be placed on popularizing chess among women and introducing modern digital technologies into the educational process. The two-day conference program will feature panel discussions, presentations of modern educational programs, and hands-on workshops led by leading specialists. Representatives of Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Education, international experts, education methodologists, and members of the teaching community will discuss the interim results of introducing chess into Kazakhstani schools and identify directions for further development. The upcoming event will mark an important step toward strengthening interdepartmental and international cooperation in children’s and youth education, as well as promoting mind sports in Kazakhstan. Date: November 12–13, 2026 Opening time: 10:00 AM Venue: Narxoz University, 55 Zhandosov Street, Almaty Media accreditation contact: +7 777 998 8820 (Alla, Kazakhstan Chess Federation Press Office) Registration: https://conf.kazchess.kz/

title: Clutch Chess: Nakamura leads after lively first day of action
summary:
Hikaru Nakamura took the early lead at the Clutch Chess: Champions Showdown tournament in Saint Louis, scoring two wins and four draws to finish day one on 4/6 points. Javokhir Sindarov follows half a point behind, while Fabiano Caruana and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu occupy third and fourth place. The opening day featured five decisive games and plenty of exciting battles. Victories will be worth increasingly more points over the next two days. | Photo: Lennart Ootes / Saint Louis Chess Club

"I pretty much outplayed them"

The Clutch Chess: Champions Showdown event kicked off on Tuesday at the Saint Louis Chess Club, with four elite GMs competing in a rapid tournament that uses an innovative scoring system. Fabiano Caruana, Hikaru Nakamura, Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu and Javokhir Sindarov will play three double round-robins over three days, with six games per player each day at a time control of 10 minutes plus a 5-second increment.

The main feature of the format, devised by Maurice Ashley, is that victories become increasingly valuable as the tournament progresses. Wins are worth one point on Tuesday, two on Wednesday and three on Thursday. Draws count for half a point on the opening day and one point on each of the following two days. The event has a total prize fund of $425,000, including a jackpot funded by the prize money allocated to drawn games.

Four of the absolute best players in the world in action! | Photo: Crystal Fuller

Hikaru Nakamura emerged as the early leader, scoring two wins and four draws to finish the first day with 4/6 points. Javokhir Sindarov also remained undefeated, collecting one win and five draws for a 3½/6 score. Fabiano Caruana stands third on 2½/6, while Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu had the toughest day of the four participants, finishing with 2/6.

Despite the gaps in the standings, all four players remain firmly in contention. With victories worth twice as much on Wednesday and three times as much on Thursday, the remaining twelve games offer plenty of opportunities to make up lost ground.

Nakamura was the most consistent performer on Tuesday, obtaining mostly favourable positions and scoring his two victories in consecutive encounters. After drawing his opening game against Caruana with black, he defeated his compatriot with white in their second meeting. He followed this up with another win, this time against Pragg, also playing white.

The early leader could have also collected a win point in his first encounter with Caruana. Playing black, Nakamura obtained a winning position and entered a queen endgame with two extra pawns. Caruana, however, managed to find a way to give perpetual check, escaping with a draw despite his material deficit.

Caruana was already in desperado mode, attempting to complicate matters by creating a passer on the kingside in an objectively lost position. In this case, his strategy worked out, as here Nakamura faltered by responding to 58.g5 with 58...hxg5?? , allowing White to force a trade of rooks on c3 with 59.Rc8+ Kb4 60.Rxc3 Kxc3 .

The point is that White will promote to a queen on h8 with check, as was seen in the game!

In this setup, Black has no way to escape the perpetual checks, and the game was agreed drawn only a few moves later.

The winning move for Black in the first diagrammed position is 58...Re3+, a crucial intermediate check that prevents White from capturing on the key c3-square. After the king moves to either side, Black can safely collect the pawn on g5, with an easily winning position.

We got to enjoy two exciting encounters between the two strongest American chess players in the world | Photo: Crystal Fuller

Nakamura's final game of the day saw him on the other side of a difficult endgame. Sindarov obtained a winning position in an encounter that eventually reached an ending with rooks, opposite-coloured bishops and passed pawns for both players. The position was far from straightforward, and Nakamura managed to hold the draw after a lengthy struggle.

This position is winning for White, but in order to convert it, Sindarov needed to figure out that he should play 63.c6! here, allowing Black to push his passer on the f-file all the way down the board - and the Uzbek star only had 20 seconds on the clock.

Sindarov played 63.Bd4? instead, allowing Black to keep the balance by eventually trading into a pure rook and bishop against rook endgame. Still, the battle was only agreed drawn after Black played his 117 th move.

Speaking to Maurice Ashley after the games, Nakamura admitted that his performance had surprised him. Given his lengthy absence from over-the-board competition, he had expected to be the most out-of-form player in the field. Instead, he felt he had generally outplayed his opponents, remarking:

I think everyone else has been super active and they should come out guns blazing, and it actually seemed the other way around. [...] I seem to be the sharpest player. To be fair, one of the players is saving their preparation, but I still felt that compared to Fabi and Pragg I pretty much outplayed them in the games that we had. So it was very surprising because I thought it would be the other way around.

The first day featured five decisive games and seven draws, although the number of peaceful results did not reflect the amount of fighting chess on display. Several encounters saw substantial changes in the evaluation, with time trouble playing an important role.

Sindarov's only victory came in his first game against Pragg. The Indian GM had obtained a promising position earlier in the encounter, but inaccuracies under time pressure allowed his opponent to equalise. The players eventually reached an opposite-coloured bishop endgame in which Pragg failed to maintain the balance. After blundering a pawn, he also ran out of time.

Pragg faltered decisively with 47.g4?? , when after 47...hxg4 48.Bf7 (48.Kg3 Kh5 is no good either), Black wins with 48...Be1. Pragg ran out of time before the winning move appeared on the move, though.

There might have followed 48...Be1 49.e5 Bxh4 50.Be6 Kh5 51.f5 gxf5 52.Bxf5 Kg5, and Black will win by making use of the two far-apart passers on the a and g-files.

A sudden blunder ended the game between the two representatives of the young generation in Saint Louis | Photo: Crystal Fuller

The other two decisive games not involving Nakamura came in the final mini-match between Caruana and Praggnanandhaa. Both players won with the black pieces, although the character of the two encounters was markedly different.

In their first meeting, Caruana managed to turn the tables in a sharp and complicated struggle, securing his only victory of the day.

Pragg was clearly for choice in the middlegame after his brilliant 21.Nc6! - in case of 21...Qxc6 White has 22.Nf6+, grabbing the queen next.

However, an inaccuracy by White on move 27 allowed Caruana to get back in the game (though Pragg was still slightly better). And a blunder on move 32 ended the game at once.

32.Qf3?? allowed Caruana to play the great-looking 32...c2 , prompting Pragg's resignation, as 33.Qxe3 fails to 33...cxd1Q+, while other alternatives would be followed by 33...c1Q+.

Correct would have been 32.Qf4, with a sharp battle ahead.

Fabiano Caruana | Photo: Lennart Ootes

Pragg bounced back in their return encounter, demonstrating how a materially balanced position with bishops of the same colour can still offer winning chances in a simplified ending.

After 57...h6! White is in zugzwang (he could go for 58.h4, but then 58...h5 would leave him equally powerless).

The bishop on d2 is defending both the pawn on a5 and the one on f4, while a king move would allow the black monarch to decisively infiltrate. Caruana played 58.Bc3 , allowing 58...Bxf4 , and Pragg had little trouble converting his advantage into a win.

The Indian GM's win was a welcome result after a difficult start to the competition, and it allowed him to finish Tuesday on a positive note.

Wednesday's games will follow the same double round-robin structure, but with each victory now worth twice as much. The increased weighting means that even a single successful mini-match could substantially alter the standings before the final day, when the scoring system will place an even greater premium on decisive results.

title: Second GM norm puts 11-year-old Shogdzhiev on course for historic achievement
summary:
Eleven-year-old Roman Shogdzhiev has earned his second grandmaster norm after scoring 6/9 at the Serbian Super League, where he represented Partizan Belgrade. The Russian youngster gained 26 rating points and now needs one more norm to secure the GM title. With eight months remaining to break Abhimanyu Mishra's age record, Shogdzhiev has a realistic chance of becoming the youngest grandmaster in history. | Photo: Eteri Kublashvili

One more norm and about 20 rating points separate the Russian prodigy from the GM title

Eleven-year-old Roman Shogdzhiev has taken another step towards becoming the youngest grandmaster in chess history. The Russian prodigy earned his second GM norm while representing Partizan Belgrade in the Serbian Super Liga, where he faced experienced opposition on the team's top board. With two norms secured and his rating approaching 2500, Shogdzhiev is now within reach of the age record set by Abhimanyu Mishra in 2021.

Shogdzhiev scored 6 points from 9 games in Serbia, collecting four wins, four draws and a single defeat. He achieved a tournament performance rating (TPR) of 2662 and gained 26.1 rating points. He did not play in the final two rounds of the competition. A second consecutive strong showing at the European Club Cup, where he scored 4½/7 on board four for Elektroprivreda, which left his live rating at 2484.1 Elo points (he is currently ranked 19 th among players aged 16 or younger).

In Serbia, the youngster's results included victories over three grandmasters rated above 2600: Bulgaria's Ivan Cheparinov (2631), India's Bharath Subramaniyam (2603) and Singapore's Tin Jingyao (2602). He also drew with eight-time Hungarian champion GM Ferenc Berkes. His only defeat came against Indian IM Santhosh Parvathareddy.

Roman Shogdzhiev's games from the 2026 Serbian Super Liga

Select an entry from the list to switch between games

The result in Serbia follows Shogdzhiev's first GM norm, achieved at the Asian Individual Championship in Ulaanbaatar in June. On that occasion, he entered the tournament as the 50 th seed and scored 6/9 points, remaining undefeated against six grandmasters. At 11 years, 4 months and 1 day, he became the youngest player ever to obtain a GM norm.

In May 2025, Shogdzhiev became the youngest international master in history, earning the title at 10 years, 3 months and 21 days. His training is overseen by a group of grandmasters led by former Russian champion Evgeny Tomashevsky. Leonard Barden noted on his latest column for The Guardian :

For several years now his team of coaches led by the experienced GM Evgeny Tomashevsky have organised periodic blitz tournaments in Moscow where the youngster could hone his speed skills against strong rivals.

The next target is the grandmaster title itself. Shogdzhiev still needs one more norm and must reach the 2500 rating threshold. The record for the youngest grandmaster currently belongs to GM Abhimanyu Mishra from the United States, who completed the title requirements in June 2021 at 12 years, 4 months and 25 days. More recently, Argentina's Faustino Oro became the second-youngest grandmaster in history, obtaining the title at 12 years, 6 months and 26 days.

Shogdzhiev has until late June 2027 to improve on Mishra's record. There is also the possibility of reaching an unprecedented milestone: should he fulfil the remaining requirements before his 12 th birthday on 4 February 2027, he would become the first player to earn the grandmaster title before turning twelve.

The Russian is part of a generation of young players who have been collecting titles and breaking age records at a remarkable pace. Another player born in 2015, England's Bodhana Sivanandan, recently became the youngest female international master in history , surpassing Judit Polgar's longstanding record.

title: KazChess Masters Almaty 2026 - Live!
summary:
The KazChess Masters Almaty 2026 takes place from 26 October to 3 November in Kazakhstan. The ten-player invitational tournament brings together five international grandmasters and five players from the host country. Among the best-known participants are Muhammad Muradli, Daniil Dubov and Denis Lazavik, who recently reached the Esports World Cup final. Another player to watch is 14-year-old Kazakh talent Mark Smirnov (pictured). | Live from approximately 6:15 AM ET / 3:45 PM IST / 11:15 AM CET | Photo: Kazakhstan Chess Federation

The KazChess Masters in Almaty is a ten-player round-robin tournament featuring players from six countries. The time control is 90 minutes for the first 40 moves, followed by 30 minutes for the rest of the game, with a 30-second increment from move one. Draw offers are not permitted before move 30.

The top seeds are Azerbaijan's Mahammad Muradli (2662) and Russian grandmaster Daniil Dubov (2654). Other international players include Shamsiddin Vokhidov of Uzbekistan, Aram Hakobyan of Armenia and Denis Lazavik of Belarus. They face five players from host nation Kazakhstan.

Among them is 14-year-old Mark Smirnov, a two-time World Youth Champion. Another player to watch is IM Alua Nurman, the only woman in the field. The remaining Kazakh participants are GMs Denis Makhnev and Edgar Mamedov, and IM Sauat Nurgaliyev.
